A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same research work, including their complete appendices. The core equations, Table 1 and all thirteen original figures can be matched across versions, including relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original gradient-descent and Adam simulations, numerical separability and margin analyses, and validation of the simplified model in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original numerical results and adds experiments on noisy two-Gaussian classification, alternative input distributions and nonconstant labels in Figures 4, 15 and 16.

M1.justification: The linear logistic classifier, loss functions and optimization procedures are retained. The zero-axis-noise two-Gaussian formulation is explicitly reduced to v1's constant-label model. The extensions change data and labeling conditions rather than introduce a new learning procedure.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's constant-label isotropic Gaussian experiments and two-point model, v2 evaluates noisy two-class Gaussian data, Gaussian inputs with power-law covariance, Gaussian-mixture inputs and threshold-generated nonconstant labels. Section 5 and Appendices G and I substantially broaden the evaluated distributions and classification scenarios.

E2.justification: No comparison method is added or removed. Existing optimizer comparisons and SVM-based asymptotic checks remain; the new experiments compare data and labeling conditions rather than competing algorithms.

E3.justification: Additional settings include lambda=0.4, mu=0.2, sigma_B=1 and learning rate 0.1 for Figure 4, and d=180, N=400 for Figure 15. The original experiments retain their stated settings and loss/accuracy metrics; these additions do not establish revisions or reruns of the earlier experiments.

E4.justification: Figures 4, 15 and 16 newly test dependence on zero separation-axis noise, isotropic Gaussian inputs and constant labels. These substantially expand robustness analysis of the mechanism's assumptions. The earlier optimizer, variance-scale, initialization and loss-function studies remain after renumbering.

E5.justification: The reported averages over 15,000, 1,000 and 100 realizations remain unchanged between v1 Appendix H and v2 Appendix K. The new experiments introduce no additional seed-reporting, confidence-interval or significance-testing practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds loss and accuracy trajectories for separation-axis noise, alternative distributions and label fractions. Figure 16, for example, reports delayed generalization with imperfect test accuracy for r=0.99 and 0.95 at lambda=0.48. The thirteen matched original figures and Table 1 retain their results; the additions are new-condition findings, not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Appendix H adds the two-Gaussian reduction and its mu-squared learning-rate scaling; Appendix I.1 derives accuracy for threshold-based labels; Appendix A broadens the stated distribution assumptions to central symmetry and general position. These extend the mathematics beyond the largely retained proofs. Proposition 3.2 also introduces an inconsistent positive-infinite bias limit.

C1.justification: The central claims about separability, the lambda=1/2 transition and arbitrarily delayed generalization remain. v2 broadens their stated setting from constant-label noise classification to two-Gaussian binary classification and makes the loss-landscape explanation more prominent.

C2.justification: Section 5 and Appendix I newly distinguish delayed generalization from eventual perfect accuracy when the constant-label or zero-axis-noise assumptions are relaxed. Appendix G extends applicability to symmetric distributions, while Section 6 explicitly qualifies that criticality elsewhere need not arise from separability. These materially revise the discussion of applicability and limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds covariance normalization, mixture-sampling and labeling instructions for the extensions. However, Appendix K drops v1 Appendix H's general Python/PyTorch implementation statement, CPU/RAM specifications and runtime disclosures. The original sample counts and most hyperparameters remain documented.

R1.justification: Related work adds discussions of Humayun et al. on delayed robustness, Golechha on progress measures and Prieto et al. on numerical stability; the discussion also cites Sethna on critical phenomena. These expand the context while retaining the original positioning around solvable grokking models and implicit bias.

P1.justification: The abstract, setup, mechanism exposition and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Existing arguments are organized into numbered propositions, a new extensions section is introduced, and the separate main-text grokking-time subsection disappears while its analysis remains in Appendix E. This is substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text, reflows existing displays and adds Figures 4, 15 and 16. v1 Figure 4 moves to Appendix E as v2 Figure 8. The original graphical results remain intact despite relocation, resizing and renumbering.

improvement.justification: The new reduction and assumption-relaxation experiments make v1's idealized constant-label mechanism more interpretable and better supported across synthetic classification settings. This gain is moderated by removed hardware/runtime disclosures and new inconsistencies, including the positive bias limit in Proposition 3.2 and Figure 15's reference to a uniform distribution despite specifying and plotting a Gaussian mixture.
